author: sky.cactus
content: I think it was timing.  Keccak256 was slated to become the sha3 standard, but there was a last minute tweak before sha3 was finalized and Ethereum already used Keccak256.

author: sky.cactus
content: I don't believe it was chosen over sha3, it was chosen in expectation of it being sha3.

author: taulepton_
content:
I think Dmitry tried to explain why its not ideal to use a standard hash such as sha3, based on the protocol's cryptographic requirements. For zk proofs we need to run fiat-shamir for which we ideally want a duplex sponge construction so that we can incrementally absorb and squeeze the hasher state. SHA-3 doesn't support this mode. However, I suppose you could use sha3 in most places with a non-standard keccak sponge construction exclusively for fiat-shamir.

There is also the motivating factor of backwards compatibility... keccak256 and sha3 use the same hashing permutation and sponge but differ only in the domain-separation instantiation by 2 bits. The EL has dependencies on keccak256 deeply enshrined in its core through things like the keccak opcode, Ethereum address computation and more generally, cryptographic commitments of protocol objects (block hash, state root, transactions root, etc.). Migrating to something like SHA-3 introduces a complexity cost, since we have to support keccak256 for backwards compatibility, so one must ask whether introducing an almost identical hash function like SHA-3 justifies the added complexity.

I'm not stating an opinion here, just expressing my understanding of the problem (which may not be correct or complete, as I haven't worked on this directly).

author: dkhovratovich
content: I would phrase it like this: We need not just a single hash function but a family of symmetric constructions (hash, duplex, PRNG, encryption) originating from one trusted component. We have selected the Keccak-1600 permutation (denote it P) as this component, as it is already widely used and extensively cryptanalyzed. The duplex construction based on P is non-standard, so it does not matter how exactly we define it. The PRNG part we will probably use standard (SHAKE). The hash function we could use standard SHA-3 (as it also P-based) or Keccak-256 (it is P-based too). The two options equal in security, the former is standard, but the latter is already deployed and has to stay in the protocol due to legacy. So as long as we can not rid of Keccak-256 completely, it makes sense to choose it over SHA-3 since it is already there. This choice would hurt if there is a library that supports SHA-3, but does not expose P. But such a library would not be sufficient anyway, except for limited usecases.

author: asn_d6
content: This choice would also hurt if, for example, a hardware wallet or a CPU decided to accelerate SHA-3 but not Keccak-256. But through our analysis, we found this very unlikely because hardware usually tries to be as generic and flexible as possible due to its immutability. So hardware would almost certainly accelerate the sub-component Keccak-1600 (P from above), and not the entire hash function box.
